subject: The use of increment_log_prob() through a simple example

messages.author: 5e0a072a41164542
messages.subject: The use of increment_log_prob() through a simple example
parts:
Hi there,

 From the Stan 2.3 manual, I found that instead of using a distribution like 
    ... 
    model {
       y~ normal(mu, sigma); 
    }
    
      Stan can run the model in the same way by using "increment_log_prob()" function and specify the log likelihood in the parentheses. Namely, we can use: 

    ... 
    model {
        increment_log_prob(normal_log(y, mu, sigma));
    }
    
    I'm not sure is my understanding is right. I ran the code and got similar parameter estimates but different lp__ , can anybody explain the reason to me?

    Also, after reading several questions and answers regarding increment_log_prob() and lp__ in the Google group, I found we can also use (if y is a vector) :
    ... 
    model {
        increment_log_prob(-0.5*dot_self(y-mu) / square(sigma));   
    }

    by dropping the terms not containing a parameter.  


    However, if my model is hierarchical, mu also follows a distribution, for example, normal(0, 2), and I still want to write it down in the increment_log_prob way, can I write:
    ... 
    model {
        increment_log_prob(normal_log(mu, 0, 2));   // or can I use   increment_log_prob(-0.5*(mu-0) / square(2))  ?
        increment_log_prob(-0.5*dot_self(y-mu) / square(sigma));   
    }

   
    I didn't found a lot of examples in the manual and want to confirm if my understandings of using "increment_log_prob()" are right. Thanks!!

Dora

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] The use of increment_log_prob() through a simple example
parts:
On Fri, Jul 11, 2014 at 5:13 PM, Dora Zhou <zhou...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hi there,

 From the Stan 2.3 manual, I found that instead of using a distribution like 
    ... 
    model {
       y~ normal(mu, sigma); 
    }
    
      Stan can run the model in the same way by using "increment_log_prob()" function and specify the log likelihood in the parentheses. Namely, we can use: 

    ... 
    model {
        increment_log_prob(normal_log(y, mu, sigma));
    }
    
    I'm not sure is my understanding is right. I ran the code and got similar parameter estimates but different lp__ , can anybody explain the reason to me?

The reason is that the first case (x ~ normal(...)) drops the irrelevant constants for speed.  (I.E., those constants that don't depend on parameters)  As a result, lp__ is different but it will be different by a constant equal to something like log(2*pi*sigma).

Also, after reading several questions and answers regarding increment_log_prob() and lp__ in the Google group, I found we can also use (if y is a vector) :
    ... 
    model {
        increment_log_prob(-0.5*dot_self(y-mu) / square(sigma));   
    }

    by dropping the terms not containing a parameter.  


    However, if my model is hierarchical, mu also follows a distribution, for example, normal(0, 2), and I still want to write it down in the increment_log_prob way, can I write:
    ... 
    model {
        increment_log_prob(normal_log(mu, 0, 2));   // or can I use   increment_log_prob(-0.5*(mu-0) / square(2))  ?
        increment_log_prob(-0.5*dot_self(y-mu) / square(sigma));   
    }

   
    I didn't found a lot of examples in the manual and want to confirm if my understandings of using "increment_log_prob()" are right. Thanks!!

All of those are equivalent and just fine.  That said, I would encourage you to use the x~normal(...) notation unless you have a good reason not to.  It will generally be faster than anything you can do by hand, particularly with something like normal_log which has been pretty well optimized.

Cheers,
Marcus
